newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: UN finds no Khmer Rouge at detention sites.
newsitem.headline: UN finds no Khmer Rouge at detention sites.

text.p: United Nations human rights workers said on Friday they had found no evidence to back Cambodian coup leader Hun Sen's claim that his rival Prince Ranariddh had brought Khmer Rouge defectors into Phnom Penh.
Hun Sen cited the presence of Khmer Rouge soldiers in Phnom Penh as the reason for ousting First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh in a bloody coup two weeks ago.
But U.N. human rights workers said on Friday they had been unable to locate any Khmer Rouge soldiers in visits to city detention centres where hundreds of troops loyal to Ranariddh were still held.

That raises the possibility Hun Sen misused the spectre of the Khmer Rouge, who terrorised Cambodia during the reign of Pol Pot from 1975-1979 and as guerrilla fighters for more than a decade afterwards, to justify his power grab.
If there were Khmer Rouge soldiers captured in the aftermath of the July 5-6 fighting they have not been accounted for.
Given that rights workers believe some 40 opposition supporters are believed to have been killed extra-judicially after the coup, Khmer Rouge soldiers taken into custody may have been killed.
"We're sticking with the number of at least 40 deaths although we have many more reports that we are investigating," said one U.N. rights worker in the Cambodian capital.
"What I think is new and of significance is that we have been unable to find any Khmer Rouge in detention. Either there never were any or they have gone missing since the fighting."

Both the United Nations and the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) have been visiting detention centres to check on the well-being of prisoners and to investigate reports of torture and extrajudicial murder.
One problem has been that the number of reported detainees fluctuates wildly from day to day and place to place.
A U.N. rights worker was told by government officials on Thursday that Tang Krasang, the former headquarters of missing Ranariddh loyalist General Nhiek Bun Chhay, held 271 prisoners.
The investigator visited the site on Friday and found only 113 prisoners there.
"We were told that all the others had escaped overnight and at first I feared for the worst," said a U.N. rights worker.
"We talked to the prisoners who remained and it then seemed pretty clear that those who left managed to buy their way out and that those left behind lacked the means to do so.
"We didn't uncover reports of vehicles coming in the middle of the night to haul people away or anything like that."
